phy-01.title: Measurement and Units
explain: Physics is the study that describes nature with **numbers and units**. "The length is 5" tells us nothing. We need to know whether it is 5 m or 5 km. A measured value is a pair of **number + unit**.

The unit system used worldwide is the **SI** (International System of Units). The three base units used most often in this course are:
- Length: meter (m)
- Mass: kilogram (kg)
- Time: second (s)
Large and small values are shortened with **prefixes**. Kilo (k) means 1000 times, centi (c) means 1/100, and milli (m) means 1/1000. $1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$.

explain: When converting units, only the **notation** changes, not the value itself. To convert the speed unit $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$, use 1 km = 1000 m and 1 h = 3600 s. So dividing the $\text{km/h}$ value by 3.6 gives the $\text{m/s}$ value.

phy-02.title: Motion
explain: **Speed** is the distance traveled per unit of time. At constant speed, $v = \dfrac{d}{t}$, and the distance is $d = vt$. The unit of speed is m/s.

On a **position-time graph**, which plots position against time, the **slope** of a straight line is the speed. The steeper the line, the faster the motion. A horizontal line means the position does not change, that is, the object is **at rest**.

explain: When the speed changes over time, there is **acceleration**. Acceleration is the change in speed per unit time, $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, and its unit is $\text{m/s}^2$. Slowing down is also a change in speed, so it counts as acceleration, just as speeding up does.

phy-03.title: Force and the Laws of Motion
explain: **Force** is the cause that changes the state of motion of an object, and its unit is the newton (N). When several forces act on one object, what matters is the **net force**, the sum of the forces taking their directions into account.

The three laws of Newton are summarized below.
- **Law of inertia**: If the net force is zero, an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving at the same velocity.
- **Law of acceleration**: $F = ma$. The larger the net force and the smaller the mass, the larger the acceleration.
- **Action-reaction law**: The force A exerts on B and the force B exerts on A are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects.

phy-04.title: Work and Energy
explain: When a force moves an object in the direction of the force, **work** is done. $W = Fd$, and its unit is the joule (J). 1 J is the work done by a force of 1 N moving an object through 1 m.

**Energy** is the ability to do work. A moving object has **kinetic energy** $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, and an object at height $h$ has **potential energy** $U = mgh$. If the speed doubles, the kinetic energy becomes four times as large.

explain: When friction and air resistance are ignored, **mechanical energy is conserved**. As height decreases, potential energy decreases, and kinetic energy increases by the same amount.

phy-05.title: Waves
explain: A **wave** is a phenomenon in which energy is transmitted while a medium vibrates. In water waves, the water itself only moves up and down in place and does not travel far along with the wave. Sound requires a medium such as air.

explain.alt: Wave-shaped diagram. The dotted line is the baseline. A wavelength mark spans between two adjacent crests, and the amplitude is labeled on a vertical line from a trough to the baseline. Below it is written: one wavelength = 2.0 m.
explain.caption: The distance between adjacent crests of a wave is one wavelength.

explain:
The quantities that describe a wave are summarized below.
- **Wavelength** $\lambda$: the distance between adjacent crests (or between adjacent troughs). Unit: m.
- **Amplitude**: the height from the baseline to a crest (or trough).
- **Frequency** $f$: the number of waves that pass in 1 second. Unit: hertz (Hz).
- **Period** $T$: the time needed for one vibration. $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$.
The speed at which a wave advances is $$v = f\lambda$$. Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.

phy-06.title: Basic Electricity
explain: The flow of electrically charged particles is the **electric current**. The unit of current is the ampere (A). phy-07.title: Momentum and Impulse: The Physics of Collisions
explain: The forces two objects exert on each other when they collide are very large, last only a very short time, and change in complicated ways. Finding these forces moment by moment from $F = ma$ is nearly impossible. Surprisingly, comparing only the situation **before and after** the collision lets us calculate the result without knowing the details of the force. The key to this is **momentum**.

Momentum is a vector defined as $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$. Writing Newton's second law in terms of momentum gives $\mathbf{F} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt}$, and integrating over time gives the **impulse** $\mathbf{J} = \int \mathbf{F}\,dt = \Delta\mathbf{p}$. For the same change in momentum, lengthening the collision time reduces the average force. Airbags and breakfalls in martial arts use this principle.

When objects A and B collide, the force A exerts on B and the force B exerts on A are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, by Newton's third law. Therefore the two impulses are also equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and the two changes in momentum add up to zero. If the net external force is zero, the **total momentum of the system is conserved**: $m_A\mathbf{v}_A + m_B\mathbf{v}_B = m_A\mathbf{v}_A' + m_B\mathbf{v}_B'$.

explain.alt: Before the collision: cart A, of mass 2 kg, moves to the right at 3 m/s, and cart B, of mass 1 kg, is at rest. After the collision: A and B stick together as one 3 kg mass moving to the right at speed v (question mark).

explain: Momentum is conserved in every collision, but **kinetic energy is not**. If kinetic energy is also conserved, the collision is an **elastic collision**. If part of it is converted into heat, sound, or deformation, it is an **inelastic collision**. If the two objects stick together, it is a **perfectly inelastic collision**. In the case in the figure, where they stick together, $v' = \frac{m_Av_A + m_Bv_B}{m_A + m_B}$, and the loss of kinetic energy is the largest.

In one-dimensional elastic collisions, solving the two conservation laws together gives the simple result that "**the magnitude of the relative velocity is the same before and after the collision**" ($v_A - v_B = -(v_A' - v_B')$). This is why a ball that hits a stationary ball of the same mass head-on in an elastic collision passes its entire velocity on and stops.

Limitations: momentum conservation is often an approximation that applies when **the collision time is short enough that external forces can be ignored**. It cannot be used for the entire process of sliding for a long time on a surface with large friction. Also, in two-dimensional collisions, momentum must be conserved separately for each component; simply adding the magnitudes gives wrong results.

body: Conditions: the situation in the figure. $m_A = 2$ kg, $v_A = 3$ m/s, and $m_B = 1$ kg at rest.

Step 2 (energy comparison): kinetic energy before the collision is $\frac{1}{2}(2)(3^2) = 9$ J, and after the collision $\frac{1}{2}(3)(2^2) = 6$ J. 3 J was converted into heat and deformation.

phy-08.title: Rotational Motion and Conservation of Angular Momentum
explain: When you open a door, pushing near the hinge makes it hard to open, while pushing the handle opens it easily. The same force has a different rotational effect depending on **where** it is applied. Rotational motion follows the same structure of laws as translational motion, but each quantity takes a "rotational version."

The quantity that expresses the rotational effect is the **torque** $\tau = rF\sin\theta$. Here $r$ is the distance from the axis of rotation to the point where the force is applied, and $\theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{F}$. The farther from the axis and the more perpendicular the push, the larger the torque. For a stationary object to neither rotate nor slide, both the sum of the forces and the sum of the torques must be zero (static equilibrium).

In translational motion, mass measures how hard it is to change the motion. In rotation, the **moment of inertia** $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$ plays that role. Even with the same mass, $I$ is larger when the mass is distributed farther from the axis. So the equation of motion for rotation is $\tau = I\alpha$ ($\alpha$ is the angular acceleration), and the rotational kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.

The quantity corresponding to momentum is the **angular momentum** $L = I\omega$. Since $\tau = \frac{dL}{dt}$, if the external torque is zero, **angular momentum is conserved**. A typical example is a figure skater pulling in her arms, which reduces $I$ and increases $\omega$. Kepler's second law (constant rate of area sweeping), in which a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun, is also a consequence of conservation of angular momentum.

It is convenient to remember the correspondence between translation and rotation as a table: position ↔ angle, velocity $v$ ↔ angular velocity $\omega$, mass $m$ ↔ moment of inertia $I$, force $F$ ↔ torque $\tau$, momentum $mv$ ↔ angular momentum $I\omega$, kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ ↔ $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. A rolling object performs both motions at once, so its kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.

Limitations: for a figure skater pulling in her arms, angular momentum is conserved, but **rotational kinetic energy increases** (seen in $\frac{L^2}{2I}$, where $I$ decreases). That energy comes from the work done when the skater pulls in the arms. It is important to distinguish quantities that are conserved from those that are not. Also, $I$ depends on the axis, so the same object has different values depending on which axis it rotates about.

Step 1 (conservation of angular momentum): $4 \times 2 = 1.6\,\omega'$, so $\omega' = 5$ rad/s.
Step 2 (energy): before, $\frac{1}{2}(4)(2^2) = 8$ J; after, $\frac{1}{2}(1.6)(5^2) = 20$ J. The extra 12 J is work done by the muscles pulling the arms in.

phy-09.title: Simple Harmonic Motion and Central-Force Orbits: Mechanics through the Lagrangian
explain: A spring, a pendulum, vibrations inside an atom, and planetary orbits look different on the surface but share the same mathematics. This lesson covers two key models, **simple harmonic motion** and **central-force orbits**, and offers a taste of the **Lagrangian** viewpoint that unifies them.

An object whose displacement $x$ from the equilibrium point is pushed back by a restoring force $F = -kx$ follows $m\ddot{x} = -kx$. The solution is $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$, with angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. **The period is independent of the amplitude.** A pendulum at a small angle also becomes simple harmonic motion if we approximate $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, with $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$. The reason motion near almost any stable equilibrium point can be approximated as simple harmonic motion is that, when the potential energy is expanded in a Taylor series around the equilibrium point, the first nontrivial term is $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

A planet is subject to a force directed toward the Sun, the **central force** $F = -\frac{GMm}{r^2}$. A central force produces no torque, so angular momentum is conserved and the motion is confined to a plane. For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, so $\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ gives $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, and the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the radius ($T^2 \propto r^3$, Kepler's third law).

Newtonian methods treat forces as vectors. **Lagrangian mechanics**, by contrast, starts from a single scalar, $L = T - V$ (kinetic energy minus potential energy). Simply substituting into the Euler-Lagrange equation $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$ yields the equation of motion. For simple harmonic motion, substituting $L = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2 - \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ immediately gives $m\ddot{x} + kx = 0$.

The advantage of the Lagrangian is that **the choice of coordinates is free**. Describing a pendulum by a single angle $\theta$ instead of Cartesian coordinates, and a planet in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$, gives the equations of motion without computing constraint forces such as the tension in a string. Moreover, if $L$ does not depend on a given coordinate, the momentum conjugate to it is conserved. For a central force, $L$ does not depend on the angle $\theta$, and this is how conservation of angular momentum follows.

Limitations: the simple harmonic approximation holds only for **small amplitudes**. As the amplitude of a pendulum grows, its period becomes longer. Also, forces that dissipate energy, such as friction, are hard to include in a basic Lagrangian. And the circular-orbit formula $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ cannot be used for the speed at every instant of an elliptical orbit.

Step 1: $\omega = \sqrt{50/0.5} = 10$ rad/s, $T = 2\pi/10 \approx 0.63$ s.
Step 2: maximum speed $v_{max} = A\omega = 1$ m/s, and mechanical energy $\frac{1}{2}kA^2 = 0.25$ J. Doubling the amplitude leaves the period unchanged, but the energy becomes four times as large.

Step 2: $T_A = 8T_B$. Since $v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$, A's speed is half of B's. The farther satellite moves more slowly along a longer path.

phy-10.title: Ideal Gases and Kinetic Theory
explain: One mole of gas contains about $6 \times 10^{23}$ molecules. It is impossible to track the motion of each of these molecules one by one. Yet the quantities we measure, such as pressure and temperature, obey remarkably simple laws. **Statistical mechanics** explains how the averages of countless microscopic motions become macroscopic laws.

Experimentally, gases of low density obey the **ideal gas equation of state** $pV = nRT$. Here $n$ is the number of moles, $R = 8.31$ J/(mol·K), and the temperature $T$ is in **kelvin**. Plugging in the Celsius temperature gives a wrong result. Written in terms of the number of molecules $N$, it becomes $pV = Nk_BT$, and $k_B = R/N_A \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is the **Boltzmann constant**.

**Kinetic theory of gases** derives this law. If molecules are treated as small balls that collide elastically with the walls, the pressure can be found by multiplying the impulse $2mv_x$ that one molecule gives the wall by the collision frequency. The result is $pV = \frac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^2}$. Comparing this with the equation of state gives $$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$$. **Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.**

From this, the **root-mean-square speed** $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ ($M$ is the molar mass) follows. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster. At 300 K, nitrogen ($M = 0.028$ kg/mol) has a speed of about 517 m/s, and hydrogen is $\sqrt{14} \approx 3.7$ times faster than that.

In the average energy $\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, the 3 is the number of directions of motion. This is an example of the **equipartition theorem**: each degree of freedom whose energy enters as a square receives an average of $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$. The internal energy of a monatomic gas is $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT$. A diatomic molecule adds 2 rotational degrees of freedom, giving $\frac{5}{2}nRT$ at room temperature.

Limitations: the ideal gas model ignores the volume of the molecules and the attraction between them. At high pressure and low temperature, when a gas nears liquefaction, the model fails badly, and the van der Waals equation corrects for this. Also, the equipartition theorem is a classical theory, so the phenomenon of vibrational degrees of freedom "freezing out" at low temperature can be explained only by quantum mechanics.

phy-11.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes
explain: When steam engines drove the Industrial Revolution, people wanted to know how much work could be obtained from heat. The first step toward that answer was the realization that heat is also a form of energy. The **first law of thermodynamics** extends the law of energy conservation to include heat.

Let $Q$ be the heat flowing into the system and $W$ be the work the system does on its surroundings. Then the change in internal energy is $\Delta U = Q - W$. Attention must be paid to the sign convention. In this lesson, **heat received by the system is positive, and work done by the system is positive** (some textbooks use the opposite convention). The internal energy $U$ is a state function that does not depend on the path, but $Q$ and $W$ **depend on the path**.

The work done by a gas as its volume changes is $W = \int p\,dV$, that is, the **area under the $p$-$V$ graph**. The net work for a cycle is the **area enclosed by the closed curve**. If the cycle runs clockwise, the system does positive work on its surroundings (a heat engine). After one full cycle the system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U = 0$, and the net heat equals the net work.

explain.alt: Graph with the horizontal axis showing volume V (L, 0 to 4) and the vertical axis showing pressure p (in units of 100 kPa, 0 to 5). A rectangular cyclic process connecting vertices A (1 L, 4), B (3 L, 4), C (3 L, 1), and D (1 L, 1) is drawn with arrows in the order A→B→C→D→A, which is clockwise.

explain: The four typical processes are: **isochoric** ($W = 0$, $Q = \Delta U$), **isobaric** ($W = p\Delta V$), **isothermal** (for an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$), and **adiabatic** ($Q = 0$, so $W = -\Delta U$; the gas cools when it expands). An adiabatic process follows $pV^\gamma = $ constant, with $\gamma = C_p/C_v$ (5/3 for a monatomic gas). Therefore, on a $p$-$V$ graph, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve.

Limitations: all of these formulas assume **quasi-static processes**, that is, processes that happen slowly enough that the system is nearly in equilibrium at every moment. **Free expansion**, in which a gas suddenly spreads into a vacuum, cannot be drawn as a curve on the graph. Since both work and heat are zero, the temperature of an ideal gas does not change. The method of finding work from the area under the graph can be used only for quasi-static processes.

examples.title: Cyclic process in the figure
body: Conditions: A→B→C→D→A in the figure. Pressure unit $100$ kPa $= 10^5$ Pa, volume unit L $= 10^{-3}$ m³.

Step 1: A→B is isobaric expansion, $W_{AB} = 4 \times 10^5 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 800$ J. C→D is isobaric compression, $W_{CD} = 1 \times 10^5 \times (-2 \times 10^{-3}) = -200$ J. The isochoric processes B→C and D→A do no work.
Step 2: Net work $= 800 - 200 = 600$ J, which equals the area of the rectangle. Since $\Delta U = 0$ over one cycle, the net heat absorbed is also 600 J.

Step 1: $W = nRT\ln 2 = 8.31 \times 300 \times 0.693 \approx 1730$ J.
Step 2: Because the process is isothermal, $\Delta U = 0$, and the absorbed heat is $Q = W \approx 1730$ J. All of the heat received left as work.

phy-12.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics: Carnot Efficiency and Entropy
explain: The first law says that energy is not destroyed, but it does not say **in which direction** energy can flow. A hot cup of coffee cools on its own, but a cooled cup of coffee never warms up by itself. Energy conservation alone cannot explain this asymmetry. The law that determines the direction is the **second law**.

There are two classical statements of the second law. **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic engine can take heat from a single heat reservoir and convert all of it into work. **Clausius**: heat cannot flow from a colder place to a hotter place without any other effect. The two statements are logically equivalent.

A heat engine with a high-temperature reservoir at $T_H$ receives $Q_H$, does work $W$, and discards heat to a low-temperature reservoir at $T_C$ in the amount $Q_C$. Its efficiency is $\eta = W/Q_H = 1 - Q_C/Q_H$. Carnot showed that a reversible engine (two isothermal processes and two adiabatic processes) has the highest efficiency between the same two temperatures: $$\eta_{Carnot} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}$$ The temperatures must be in kelvin. No technology can exceed this limit.

For reversible processes, Clausius defined $dS = \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T}$ as the **entropy** $S$. The second law can be written as "**the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease**" ($\Delta S \ge 0$), with equality holding only for reversible processes. When heat $Q$ flows from $T_H$ to $T_C$, $\Delta S = -\frac{Q}{T_H} + \frac{Q}{T_C} > 0$. In the reverse direction the total would be negative, which is forbidden.

Boltzmann revealed the microscopic meaning of entropy: $S = k_B \ln \Omega$. Here $\Omega$ is the number of microstates that produce the same macrostate. For example, the number of arrangements of 100 coins with 50 heads is overwhelmingly larger than the number with 100 heads (only 1 arrangement). A system moves toward larger entropy because **the microstates on that side are overwhelmingly numerous**. It is a probabilistic tendency.

Limitations and misconceptions: the increase of entropy is a statement about the **entire isolated system**. Local decreases of entropy, as in a refrigerator or a living organism, are possible because they export more entropy to the surroundings. Also, understanding entropy merely as "disorder" leads to errors. Its precise meaning is "the number of possible microstates."

Step 1: Converting to kelvin, $T_H = 800$ K and $T_C = 300$ K.

Step 2: $\eta_{max} = 1 - 300/800 = 0.625$. Real power plants are far below this because of friction and irreversible heat transfer. Computing $1 - 27/527$ with Celsius values gives 0.95, which is wrong.

phy-13.title: Electric Fields, Electric Potential, and Gauss's Law
explain: In Stage 1 we calculated the force between two charges using Coulomb's law. But when there are countless charges, or when charge is spread continuously over a sphere, a plate, or a wire, adding up the forces between every pair quickly becomes unmanageable. This lesson learns how to solve such problems using the concepts of the **field** and **symmetry**.

The **electric field** $\mathbf{E}$ is the force a test charge $q$ would feel if placed at each point in space, divided by $q$: $\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{F}/q$. The electric field of a point charge $Q$ is $E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$ ($k \approx 9 \times 10^9$ N·m²/C²), pointing outward. The electric fields of several charges are **added** as vectors (superposition principle).

**Gauss's law** states that the electric flux passing outward through a closed surface is proportional to the charge enclosed by it: $$\oint \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = \frac{Q_{in}}{\varepsilon_0}$$ The key point is that **charges outside the surface do not contribute to the flux**, because the field lines that enter the surface leave it again. For highly symmetric cases, $E$ is constant over the surface, and the integral turns into a multiplication.

Results by symmetry: **spherical symmetry** (outside a uniformly charged sphere) gives $E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$, the same as if the charge were concentrated at the center. **Cylindrical symmetry** (an infinitely long straight line with linear charge density $\lambda$) gives $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, inversely proportional to distance. **Planar symmetry** (an infinite plane with surface charge density $\sigma$) gives $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, independent of distance. Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, $E = 0$, and all the charge lies on the surface.

Looking at the problem in terms of energy instead of force leads to the **electric potential** (electrostatic potential) $V$. It is potential energy per unit charge; for a point charge, $V = \frac{kQ}{r}$. Potential is a scalar and therefore easy to add, while the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential ($E = -\frac{dV}{dx}$). When a charge $q$ moves through a potential difference $\Delta V$, its kinetic energy changes by $q\Delta V$. The energy an electron gains passing through 1 V is 1 eV $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

Limitations: Gauss's law is **always true**, but **without symmetry** it is of little use for finding the electric field. The field of a cube-shaped charge distribution cannot be found from Gauss's law alone. Also, it is a common mistake to think that "zero flux through a closed surface" means "zero electric field on that surface."

Step 1 (choose the symmetry): Taking a spherical surface of radius 0.3 m as the Gaussian surface, $E$ is constant over the surface.
Step 2: $E = kQ/r^2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-9}/0.09 = 200$ N/C. Inside the metal sphere (a conductor), it is 0.

phy-14.title: RC Circuits, Magnetic Fields, and Electromagnetic Induction
explain: The circuit in Stage 1 carried a constant direct current. But circuits whose behavior **changes over time**, such as camera flashes, pacemakers, and computer memory, are in fact more important in practice. A changing current produces a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field in turn produces a current. This lesson deals with electromagnetism that involves time variation.

Connecting a capacitor $C$ and a resistor $R$ in series to a source $\mathcal{E}$, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives $\mathcal{E} = IR + \frac{q}{C}$, with $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$. This is a first-order linear differential equation of the kind handled in Stage 5, and its solution is $$V_C(t) = \mathcal{E}\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$$. The **time constant** $\tau = RC$ is the time it takes for the capacitor voltage to reach about $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\%$ of its final value.

explain.alt: Horizontal axis: time t (s, 0 to 10). Vertical axis: capacitor voltage (V, 0 to 10). The curve starts at 0 and flattens out, approaching the dashed line at the source voltage of 10 V. A point at (2 s, 6.3 V) is marked.

explain: Current produces a **magnetic field**. The magnetic field around a long straight wire is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, and its direction is found by the right-hand rule. A charge moving in a magnetic field experiences the **Lorentz force** $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$. This force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work; it only changes the direction of motion, making the charge move in a circle.

Faraday discovered the reverse effect. When the **magnetic flux** $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$ through a circuit changes, an induced electromotive force $\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$ arises. The minus sign is **Lenz's law**: the induced current flows in the direction that **opposes** the change in flux. Generators, transformers, wireless chargers, and induction cooktops all work on this principle.

Limitations: the RC formula holds when the resistor and capacitor are ideal and the inductance of the wires themselves is neglected. For very fast signals this assumption breaks down. Also, the sign in Lenz's law is directly tied to energy conservation. If the induced current flowed in the direction that aids the change, then merely nudging a magnet would make the current and motion grow without end, violating energy conservation.

examples.title: Reading the time constant from a graph
body: Conditions: the charging curve in the figure, source voltage 10 V, and capacitor $C = 100\ \mu$F.
Step 1: The time to reach 6.3 V, which is 63% of the final value, is 2 s, so $\tau = 2$ s.
Step 2: $R = \tau/C = 2 / (100 \times 10^{-6}) = 20{,}000\ \Omega$. After about $5\tau = 10$ s, the capacitor is more than 99% charged, and we regard it as essentially full.

Step 1: The change in flux is $\Delta\Phi = 0 - 0.5 \times 0.02 = -0.01$ Wb.
Step 2: $|\mathcal{E}| = 0.01/0.1 = 0.1$ V. By Lenz's law, the induced current flows in the direction that supports the decreasing magnetic field.

phy-15.title: Maxwell's Equations and Electromagnetic Waves
explain: Until the mid-nineteenth century, electricity, magnetism, and light were considered separate phenomena. While organizing the laws of electricity and magnetism into four equations, Maxwell noticed that one term was **missing**. When he filled that gap, the nature of light was revealed. It is one of the greatest unifications in the history of physics.

Maxwell's equations (integral form, in vacuum): ① Gauss's law $\oint \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = Q_{in}/\varepsilon_0$: charge is the source of the electric field. ② Gauss's law for magnetism $\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = 0$: there are no magnetic monopoles, and magnetic field lines are closed. ③ Faraday's law $\oint \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$: a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. ④ Ampère–Maxwell law $\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = \mu_0 I + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$: current and a **changing electric field** produce a magnetic field.

The last term of ④, the **displacement current**, is the term Maxwell added. Consider a capacitor being charged. No charge flows between its plates, but the electric field changes. Without this term, Ampère's law would give different answers depending on how the surface bounded by the loop is chosen, a contradiction. The displacement current resolves this contradiction and at the same time completes the symmetry.

Now consider ③ and ④ together. A changing magnetic field produces an electric field, and a changing electric field in turn produces a magnetic field. So in empty space with no charge, the two fields can generate each other and propagate outward. Solving the equations, the speed of this **electromagnetic wave** is $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} \approx 3.0 \times 10^8$ m/s. The two constants measured in electric and magnetic experiments gave the already known speed of light. Maxwell concluded that **light is an electromagnetic wave**.

An electromagnetic wave is a **transverse wave**. $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are perpendicular to each other, both are perpendicular to the direction of travel, and their magnitudes are related by $E/B = c$. Since the general wave relation $c = f\lambda$ holds, the **electromagnetic spectrum**, divided by frequency into radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays, is all the same phenomenon.

Limitations: Maxwell's theory treats light as a continuous wave. This picture explains diffraction and interference perfectly, but it cannot explain the **photoelectric effect** that we will see in the next stage. Also, the ether assumed by the idea that "a wave must have a medium" was not confirmed by experiment, and this problem led to special relativity.

phy-16.title: Special Relativity: Time Dilation and Mass-Energy
explain: Maxwell's equations give the speed of light $c$ as a constant. But relative to whom is it $c$? One might expect light shone forward from a moving train to travel at $c$ plus the train's speed as seen from the ground. Experiments (such as Michelson–Morley) showed this is not the case. Einstein resolved this contradiction by changing the concepts of time and space.

The two postulates of special relativity: ① **Principle of relativity**: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames moving at constant velocity. ② **Constancy of the speed of light**: in a vacuum, the speed of light is $c$ regardless of the motion of the source or the observer. All the results follow logically from these two statements.

Let us derive time dilation using a **light clock**. Light bouncing between two mirrors separated by a distance $d$ takes $\Delta t_0 = 2d/c$ for one tick of a clock at rest. If this clock moves at speed $v$, a stationary observer sees the light travel a longer, slanted path. Calculating with the Pythagorean theorem and the constancy of the speed of light gives $$\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0, \quad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$$. **A moving clock runs slow.** The time measured by an observer moving together with the clock, such as $\Delta t_0$, is called the **proper time**.

The same logic shows that lengths along the direction of motion shrink to $L = L_0/\gamma$ (**length contraction**), and events that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another (**relativity of simultaneity**). The proper lifetime of cosmic-ray muons is about $2.2\ \mu$s, so even at the speed of light they should travel only about 660 m. But because $\gamma$ is very large, they descend several kilometers to the ground. This is direct evidence of time dilation.

Mechanics changes as well. Momentum is $p = \gamma mv$ and energy is $E = \gamma mc^2$. Even at rest there is a **rest energy** $E_0 = mc^2$, and the kinetic energy is $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$. When $v \ll c$, this reduces to $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ (by Taylor expansion). The release of energy equal to the mass lost in nuclear reactions is the major confirmation of $E = mc^2$.

Limitations and misconceptions: special relativity deals with **inertial frames** and with situations **without gravity**. Acceleration and gravity belong to general relativity. Also, "an object with mass cannot reach $c$" is due to $\gamma \to \infty$, not because the mass actually becomes infinitely large. In modern physics, $m$ is used as the invariant rest mass.

phy-17.title: The Photoelectric Effect and Matter Waves: The Duality of Light and Particles
explain: When light shines on a metal, electrons are ejected. If light were only a wave, even weak light would eventually accumulate enough energy over time to release electrons, and brighter light would give the electrons higher energies. The experimental results were exactly the opposite. This contradiction opened the door to quantum mechanics.

Observations: ① If the frequency of the light is lower than the **threshold frequency** $f_0$ specific to each metal, **not one** electron comes out, no matter how bright the light is. ② If $f > f_0$, electrons come out **immediately**, even with very weak light. ③ The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons depends **only on the frequency**, while brightness only increases the **number** of electrons.

Einstein's explanation: light is a stream of particles with energy $E = hf$, called **photons** ($h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s). One photon gives its entire energy to one electron. For the electron to escape from the metal, it needs energy equal to the **work function** $\phi$, so $$K_{max} = hf - \phi$$. Below $f_0 = \phi/h$, the energy of a single photon is insufficient, and no matter how many photons arrive, they cannot help.

explain.alt: Horizontal axis: frequency of light (in units of 10¹⁴ Hz, 0 to 12). Vertical axis: maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (eV, 0 to 3). For frequencies up to 5 the kinetic energy is 0. From 5 onward a straight line rises and passes through the point (10, 2.07).

explain: Graphically, $K_{max}$ is a straight line in $f$, and **the slope is Planck's constant $h$, which does not depend on the metal**. The horizontal intercept is $f_0$, and the vertical intercept (on the extended line) is $-\phi$. Changing the metal only shifts the line in parallel and does not change its slope. Measuring the slope of this line became the experiment that measures $h$.

De Broglie asked the reverse question: if light, a wave, behaves like a particle, might particles behave like waves? He assigned to a particle with momentum $p$ a **matter wave** of wavelength $\lambda = h/p$. When electrons were fired at a crystal, they did indeed produce diffraction patterns like those of X-rays. Electron microscopes use the short wavelengths of matter waves to see objects far smaller than light can resolve. For a baseball, $p$ is so large that its wavelength is unimaginably small, and its wave nature never shows.

phy-18.title: The Schrödinger Equation and the Infinite Potential Well
explain: If a particle is a wave, what equation does that wave obey? And what does the wave mean? The Schrödinger equation and Born's probability interpretation answer these two questions, and modern quantum mechanics began.

The **time-independent Schrödinger equation** for a stationary state with definite energy $E$ in one dimension is $$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + V(x)\psi = E\psi$$ ($\hbar = h/2\pi$). The first term corresponds to kinetic energy and the second to potential energy. The **wave function** $\psi(x)$ itself cannot be measured directly. $|\psi(x)|^2\,dx$ is the **probability** of finding the particle near $x$ (Born interpretation). Therefore we **normalize** the wave function so that the total probability equals 1.

The simplest example is the **infinite potential well**. A particle is confined in a box: over an interval of width $L$, $V = 0$, and outside it, $V = \infty$. Since $\psi = 0$ must hold outside the walls, the **boundary conditions** $\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0$ arise. Inside the box, the equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients, $\psi'' = -k^2\psi$ ($k^2 = 2mE/\hbar^2$), so the solutions are $\sin kx$ and $\cos kx$.

The boundary condition $\psi(0) = 0$ removes the $\cos$ term, and $\psi(L) = 0$ requires $\sin kL = 0$, that is, $kL = n\pi$ ($n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$). This is **quantization**. The energy is $$E_n = \frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2}$$, and only discrete values are allowed. It is the same principle as a guitar string fixed at both ends, which produces only specific frequencies. $n = 0$ gives $\psi = 0$, which means there is no particle, so it is not allowed. Therefore **even the ground-state energy is not zero** (zero-point energy).

Some consequences: the energy gaps grow in proportion to $n^2$, spreading out at higher levels. The **smaller** the box ($L$), the larger the energy, which scales as $1/L^2$. This is why the color of a quantum dot changes with its size. Also, in the $n = 2$ state, $|\psi|^2 = 0$ at the center of the box, creating a node where the probability of finding the particle is zero. A classical particle would have had the same probability everywhere.

Limitations: the infinite well is an idealization. Real walls have finite height, and then the wave function leaks slightly into the wall, producing the **tunnel effect**. Also, this lesson covers only one-dimensional, non-relativistic cases. Three-dimensional problems, such as an electron in an atom where $V$ goes as $1/r$, are solved by the same method, but the calculation is much longer.

Step 2: The photon energy emitted in the $n = 3 \to 2$ transition is $4.5 - 2 = 2.5$ eV. Using $E = hf$ from Lesson 6, we can find the frequency of the emitted light.

Step 2: The spacing between levels also becomes 4 times as large, so the frequency of light emitted in transitions rises (toward blue). This is why smaller quantum dots emit bluish light.

phy-19.title: Comprehensive Problem Solving: From Roller Coasters to Atoms
explain: The first lesson of the capstone stage is practice in **applying laws from several fields in succession within one scene**. Real physics problems do not arrive sorted into "formulas from this unit." At each stage you must judge for yourself which conservation law holds and which approximation is valid.

**Scene 1 (mechanics)**: A cart of mass 500 kg starts from rest at a height of 20 m and descends to the ground without friction. From conservation of mechanical energy, $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 20} \approx 19.8$ m/s. Momentum conservation cannot be used here, because gravity is an external force.

**Scene 2 (collision)**: The cart strikes an empty cart of the same mass that is at rest on the ground, and they connect. Because the collision moment is short, external forces can be ignored, so this time we use **conservation of momentum**. $v' = 19.8/2 = 9.9$ m/s. Half of the kinetic energy disappears. Of the initial energy $mgh = 500 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 98{,}000$ J, 49,000 J is converted into heat and deformation.

**Scene 3 (heat)**: If all 49,000 J heats a steel buffer of mass 20 kg (specific heat 450 J/(kg·K)), then $\Delta T = Q/(mc) = 49{,}000/(20 \times 450) \approx 5.4$ K. By the second law, this heat cannot all be converted back into the motion of the cart.

**Scene 4 (electromagnetism)**: To stop the remaining motion, place magnets along the rail to apply **eddy-current braking**. The change in magnetic flux through the moving metal plate produces an induced current, and by Lenz's law a force opposing the motion appears. Because the braking force is proportional to the speed, the velocity decreases exponentially as $v(t) = v_0e^{-t/\tau}$. This has the same structure as the first-order linear differential equation for RC-circuit charging.

**Scene 5 (transition to quantum physics)**: If atoms in the buffer are excited by heat, the emitted light is fixed by $\Delta E = hf$. At room temperature, however, the thermal energy per atom is about $k_BT \approx 0.026$ eV, far too small to emit a visible-light photon (about 2 eV). So a buffer heated only to about 5 K does not glow. **Comparing energy scales** to judge which theory is needed is part of physical reasoning.

**Critique**: Let us check the approximations in each scene. Ignoring friction breaks down if the rail is long. Conservation of momentum in a collision is valid only when the collision time is short. The assumption that heat stays in the buffer ignores heat leaking into the air and the rail. Stating the conditions under which each approximation fails is as important as the calculation.

body: While descending: the external force (gravity) does work, so the momentum changes; only conservative forces act, so mechanical energy is conserved.
At the moment of collision: internal forces dominate and the time is short, so momentum is conserved and kinetic energy is not.
During braking: a non-conservative force (the magnetic braking force) does work, so mechanical energy turns into heat, and the velocity is found from a differential equation.

phy-20.title: Capstone: Design and Critique of an Integrated Physical Model
explain: The task of the final lesson is to **analyze a phenomenon of your own choosing with a physics model from start to finish**. Where the previous lesson followed a given scene, this time you design the scene yourself.

The standard procedure for a physics model: ① **Define the system and its boundary**: what is inside the system and what is outside it. ② **Choose the governing laws**: which of the conservation laws (energy, momentum, angular momentum, charge), equations of motion, thermodynamic laws, Maxwell's equations, or quantum conditions are needed. ③ **Choose approximations**: neglecting friction, small angles, ideal gas, quasi-static, non-relativistic, and so on. ④ **Calculate**. ⑤ **Verify**: units, limits, and order-of-magnitude estimates.

Use three verification tools. **Dimensional analysis**: are the units of the result correct? If kg remains in a speed formula, the formula is wrong. **Limit checks**: if you send the mass to 0, friction to infinity, or the speed close to $c$, does the result agree with intuition? **Order-of-magnitude estimate (Fermi estimate)**: is the result wrong by a factor of 10 or 100?

In a critique, state the **range of validity of an approximation** in numbers. "We neglected air resistance" is weaker than "Because the speed is below 10 m/s, the air-resistance force is less than 1% of the weight, so we neglected it." Similarly, base your reasoning on comparisons of scale, such as "$v/c < 0.01$, so non-relativistic" or "$k_BT \ll \Delta E$, so thermal excitation is negligible."
The task of this lesson is not graded. The text you submit is saved only on this device, and you can review it under "My progress" in "Notes I left."

examples.title: Model example: a bicycle going downhill and braking
body: System: bicycle and rider (80 kg). Laws: energy conservation (downhill), work–energy theorem (braking), first law of thermodynamics (heating of the brake pads).
Approximations: air resistance neglected (at speeds up to 8 m/s the drag is about 10 N, a few percent of the slope component of gravity), rolling resistance neglected.

Calculation: going down a 3 m height gives $v = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 3} \approx 7.7$ m/s, and the kinetic energy is about 2350 J. If all of it goes into a 0.1 kg aluminum pad (specific heat 900), the temperature rises by about 26 K.
Critique: heat escapes through the rim and into the air, so the actual rise is smaller. On a long downhill, repeated heating can make this approximation dangerously wrong.

examples.title: Model example: water in a microwave oven
body: System: 0.25 kg of water. Laws: absorption of electromagnetic wave energy, first law of thermodynamics. Approximations: absorbed power constant at 700 W, heat loss neglected.
Calculation: in 60 s, 42,000 J, and $\Delta T = 42{,}000/(0.25 \times 4186) \approx 40$ K.

Critique: the energy of a single 2.45 GHz photon is about $10^{-5}$ eV, which cannot break chemical bonds. Heating is a collective effect in which countless photons increase the rotational and collisional motion of the water molecules.
